#39206. Latest Update: How we built ChatGPT’s novel ad stack for user trust and relevance

📅 21 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2981 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: How we built ChatGPT’s novel ad stack for user trust and relevance

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2981 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Ritendra Datta and Karthik Gopalratnam, Members of Technical Staff.
  • Industry observers note that traditional advertising systems are built to respond to discrete units of user intent.
  • In a recent development, our ads system supports the nuance of evolving user goals by making three key design decisions: 1) implementing stateful ads sessions, meaning information is remembered across turns of a conversation and across multiple conversations, 2) relying on a custom, post-trained LLM that uses a tool call architecture to interpret a conversation’s context and underlying intent, and then effectively select, rank, and deliver ads, and 3) running the ads selection process separately from ChatGPT’s answer generation, in its own service, to keep ads from influencing answers and maintain ChatGPT’s neutral voice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ritendra Datta and Karthik Gopalratnam, Members of Technical Staff.

Industry observers note that traditional advertising systems are built to respond to discrete units of user intent. A user searches for or views something online, the ads system receives those queries and page views as events, and the system looks for matching ads based on those events. Building an ads stack for ChatGPT was different: user intent develops across conversations and shifts over multiple turns of a conversation, sometimes without a fitting advertising moment. To support this new paradigm, we built a bespoke ads delivery system. This new type of ad stack is based on a custom, post-trained frontier LLM that makes tool calls for retrieval (identifying the top options), ranking (predicting user engagement), relevance (evaluating the usefulness of the ad), and running auctions for final ad selection and pricing.

In a recent development, our ads system supports the nuance of evolving user goals by making three key design decisions: 1) implementing stateful ads sessions, meaning information is remembered across turns of a conversation and across multiple conversations, 2) relying on a custom, post-trained LLM that uses a tool call architecture to interpret a conversation’s context and underlying intent, and then effectively select, rank, and deliver ads, and 3) running the ads selection process separately from ChatGPT’s answer generation, in its own service, to keep ads from influencing answers and maintain ChatGPT’s neutral voice. We use our post-trained LLM to orchestrate the entire ads flow, determining the right ad to surface at the right time based on both the user’s current turn and conversation history. While bootstrapping a self-improving ads system like this used to take years, ChatGPT Ads reached $1 billion in annualized revenue run rate less than 200 days after launch; now, more than 100,000 advertisers have run ads on ChatGPT since launch.

In a recent development, A conventional advertising request usually starts with a well-defined event. A user submits a search query or opens a webpage and the ads system receives a request. This type of system is fairly simple: it retrieves potential ad candidates, ranks them, runs an auction to appropriately price the opportunity, and reveals the resulting ad to the user. ChatGPT does not naturally produce such a concrete moment.

According to recent reports, in a ChatGPT conversation, people arrive with goals rather than a one-answer search query. They might be planning a trip, choosing software for their business, furnishing a home, or learning a fresh hobby. This doesn’t all happen in one turn of a conversation. ChatGPT often helps the user clarify what matters along the way.

As an example, our engineering team asked ChatGPT how to train for a race: A conversation begins with a general question about running. Several turns later, they ask about shoes to help train. The commercial meaning of the conversation changes as each constraint arrives—and this personalized context evolves across multiple sessions. A system that acted on the first message could retrieve the wrong intent entirely, potentially degrading the user’s experience and getting in their way.

Building our ads system required us to move beyond the request-response advertising architecture and build an ads stack from scratch to find potential economic opportunities while prioritizing user trust and value.

Industry observers note that turning every message into a standalone request, like a traditional ads system, would have carried a few risks in our chat use case: 1) misreading the user goal by oversimplifying it, 2) beginning the advertising flow too soon, before the user’s real need has become clear, 3) showing ads that get in the way of the user journey instead of supporting it, and 4) inefficiently rerunning the ads flow every time the request changes, creating noise and wasting cost. Instead of building around individual events, the ads system (consisting of retrieval, ranking, and delivery) maintains a stateful session, meaning the ads session runs for the duration of an eligible turn, remembering and updating information as it evolves. ChatGPT sends the initial request context to the ads server. The ads system follows and adapts to the developing exchange rather than relying on a single flattened query.

The ads selection process runs alongside ChatGPT’s normal response generation to ensure the ads flow doesn’t influence ChatGPT’s responses. Ads are filtered and selected through a separate system consuming the conversation under its own eligibility, quality, and delivery constraints. This important architectural boundary—different services that use separate models and separate code—lets core ChatGPT servers handle generating the organic response; meanwhile, the ads system independently evaluates whether there’s an appropriate advertising opportunity and, if so, prepares a sponsored placement through a separate serving process.

Advertising runs alongside the ChatGPT answer path.

According to recent reports, beyond protecting the user experience, this separation has some practical consequences. ChatGPT has no dependency on the ads system—the services are in no way intertwined and don’t share a content generation model. So if the ads serving system is unavailable or slow, ChatGPT’s organic response continues unaffected. This means the ads system can’t take down or delay the ChatGPT product. The other benefit of this separation is that it keeps the bar very high for valuable ads. Returning no ad is an ordinary, successful outcome. The system only delivers an ad if it’s clearly beneficial to people and advertisers.

The other key architectural component in our ads stack is the post-trained LLM that interprets conversations and runs the entire ads flow in an agentic loop—making tool calls to the core functions of the ads system, from the retrieval stage to ranking to auction and, ultimately, delivery. We call this LLM the orchestrator.

The first part of an ads flow is understanding user intent to start the retrieval process, which is a fast and deliberately broad sourcing of potential ads to later filter through. Receiving the conversation incrementally creates a richer but more ambiguous retrieval problem because the ads system needs to distinguish current intent from stale context. The orchestrator must interpret references to earlier messages, recognize when a user is speaking hypothetically, and avoid treating every mention of a product or service as a request to buy something.

The ads orchestrator uses the available conversation and user context, iterating to find good ads and repeatedly choosing when to call which tool with the underlying goal of finding the most appropriate ad (the ad that balances high user value and high advertiser value) for that conversation and context. If the user chooses to personalize ads, the orchestrator also considers available nonsensitive information about the user’s past conversations to find the best ad matches.

The ads orchestrator iteratively calls ads delivery tools to find valuable ads.

As the conversation progresses and the ads orchestrator gets more updated information, the orchestrator can run a fresh set of tool calls with the updated context to find better ads and return them to the client, which can then use these latest ads if they arrive in time.

The orchestrator is designed to balance user value and advertiser value, always putting people first.

Sources indicate that the ads system consists of individual tools, and the orchestrator calls them iteratively to find the best ads for a conversation. At a high level, the orchestrator turns conversations into brief text summaries, which are then turned into semantic embeddings (stored meanings that are easier for an ads system to sift through), retrieves ad candidates using those semantic embeddings, filters those candidates for eligibility (based on budget, user settings, and other preliminary checks), assesses their quality and relevance, and does a final ranking to identify high value opportunities for placement at the end of a chat response. Each ad must therefore meet a high bar on eligibility and relevance in order to be eligible for placement.

Sources indicate that the orchestrator LLM first prepares one or more queries representing the relevant commercial intent. This can include rewriting conversation context to broaden the commercial possibilities beyond 1:1 search queries and then creating semantic representations, where the orchestrator distills a multiturn conversation into a summarized version for the retrieval system—retrieving ads from our database in a focused way.

Industry observers note that ad placements will be better for both people and advertisers if they only appear when there’s deep understanding of the user’s intent. Multiple queries can preserve different aspects of intent. A conversation about planning a trip, for example, might contain distinct needs related to transportation, lodging, or activities. The retrieval system can preserve these distinctions rather than compressing the entire conversation into one literal string.

As an example, let’s look at a potential conversation sequence about hiking shoes:.

What should I cover on a two-day trip to Yosemite?

New [insert brand] product lines?

Industry observers note that although the user hasn’t connected the shoe brand question to the Yosemite trip, this conversation might be represented in our ads system by two queries, such as [shoes appropriate for hiking trip] and [latest [brand] product lines good for travel]. This might only be the first attempt; the orchestrator is designed to iterate on these representations until it finds ads in our inventory that are highly valuable to the user.

Retrieval is the process of creating a deliberately broad pool of ad options. Candidates may come from different retrieval strategies and can later compete under the same serving constraints. We build multiple indices that optimize for different system and product constraints (for example, the index for product feed ads is designed to be aware of positive or negative product reviews as it fetches the best possible ads. This is not relevant to other ads that may not have reviews associated with them). Each index is optimized for some version of approximate-nearest-neighbor (ANN) search, using embeddings representing the user’s intent. This ANN search is an approximation algorithm for retrieval over large semantic indices, meaning ads are fetched very rapidly, getting close to a good solution rather than looking for “the right” solution, while retaining most of the relevant candidates.

The ads system uses rewritten queries to create semantic embeddings during the ad retrieval process and produce a broad pool of ad candidates.

The goal of filtering is to eliminate all ad candidates from consideration that don't meet the bar for placement when it comes to relevance, bids, and budget. Depending on the candidate and configuration, filtering checks can include creative and campaign availability (whether the campaign or ad-creatives are active), campaign targeting (e.g., which locales a campaign is allowed to operate in), policy restrictions (compliance requirements around what can be advertised), budget availability (whether or not a campaign still has budget available to spend), pacing (whether a campaign should be spending budget now versus another time in the day), placement compatibility (what kinds of conversations this advertisement is eligible for), and advertiser and campaign level deduplication (picking an appropriate number of ads per advertiser to ensure fair participation across businesses).

Industry observers note that candidates that survive eligibility checks move on to a scoring phase, where the orchestrator makes tool calls to various scoring systems—for serving considerations such as semantic relevance (is the ad relevant to the user’s goal?), predicted engagement (is the ad likely to get viewed, clicked, and converted into the advertiser’s desired outcome?), historical performance (has the ad performed well when shown to users so far?). The orchestrator also filters ads to ensure relevance and safety before the auction. These systems narrow the field into a smaller candidate pool ready for auction, but they still don’t determine the final delivered ad.

According to recent reports, the orchestrator evaluates the prepared candidates in the context of the conversation and chooses which ad candidates are plausible enough to enter the final auction. The orchestrator doesn’t directly decide which ad will be served, nor does it set a price. It nominates contextually appropriate candidates for the auction tool to evaluate.

The auction applies the final serving mechanics, including auction admission (passing a minimum threshold of relevance and value), pacing (spending ad budget more evenly), bid and auction-feature computation, quality-adjusted ranking, pricing, and final selection.

After the auction, there are two ways an ad might fail to deliver, both specific to the ChatGPT conversational medium.

The ad might not feel appropriate in the chat: Even though the conversation itself was deemed safe for ad placement by integrity models (the models that decide when it’s appropriate to serve an ad), and the ad itself was deemed policy-compliant, sometimes the ad might feel inappropriate in the context of certain conversations. The orchestrator blocks these ads from being shown.

The ad request might not arrive in time: If the ChatGPT model is ready to respond, but the ad is not yet ready to place, the ad request times out and the ad doesn’t get delivered. One goal of the ads system, therefore, is to run as fast as possible. The ChatGPT model response time is dynamic, and we don’t delay chat responses to wait for ads to load.

It has been revealed that if all of the above checks are met, we send the ad to the frontend for rendering. We consider this a server-side ad delivery, but we still might not show the ad to the user—and this is by design.

It has been revealed that in a conversational product like ChatGPT, server-side delivery of an ad creative does not guarantee an ad will be displayed; the ad must also arrive in time to be included in the current turn. The ad creative includes the title, description, destination link, and any call to action. Additionally, a model-generated preamble, which is a short, neutral introduction explaining how the ad relates to the conversation, is also returned by the ads system. Keeping the preamble separate from the creative preserves the advertiser’s message while keeping ChatGPT’s voice neutral.

According to recent reports, the ChatGPT frontend receives the preamble and ad creative as a bundle. If it arrives before ChatGPT's response is fully generated, the frontend displays the ad below ChatGPT’s response, clearly labeled as sponsored. If it arrives too late, the ad is not shown for that turn. This is the difference between server-side ad delivery and a user-facing ad impression.

In a recent development, winner selection and delivery are separate events. A selected ad becomes a delivery only after ChatGPT approves and displays the placement and the delivery is acknowledged.

Our advertising stack uses traditional logging and data pipelines, which have three main benefits: advertisers can more easily integrate their existing systems with our stack, advertisers can improve their strategies with the reporting data, and our team can find areas of the system to improve. Beyond these reporting and optimization tools, we deploy a high quality model to evaluate our delivery and train other ads models, creating a powerful self-improvement loop.

According to recent reports, detailed breakdowns of what happened help us understand and improve each part of the ad system in isolation. The logs processing system also records granular outcomes such as:.

The turn was not eligible for advertising.

An ads session started but no retrieval was requested.

Retrieval returned no candidates.

Candidates were retrieved but failed hydration or eligibility.

An ad was delivered and later received an interaction.

Recent findings suggest that these detailed breakdowns help us improve each part of the ad serving system in isolation. Improving opportunity detection requires different evidence from improving retrieval, candidate quality, auction participation, or delivery reliability.

It has been revealed that delivery, serving, and quality systems observe a different part of the lifecycle. Privacy-controlled processing determines what may be used for measurement and model improvement.

Industry observers note that the idea behind model-based evaluation is that our strongest, highest-reasoning models watch and judge the results of our system, then improve the post-trained LLM by training it to perform better. For instance, we can use smaller, more efficient models or lower-reasoning models for orchestration or retrieval if our most powerful model gathers feedback and trains these small workers to do the best job possible.

Recent findings suggest that we gather and act on human feedback (clicks and hides from customers), as well as surveys for users and direct feedback from advertisers through our Ads Manager. We also make our team available for feedback as we build, and directly listen to what both ChatGPT users and advertisers want. This source of feedback informs our direction even more than the model’s observational feedback and is part of what allowed us to iterate toward the right product decisions swiftly. The model may be able to understand user intent and think critically to deliver something valuable, but people shape taste.

Recent findings suggest that A year ago, we had no ads system and only a few people thinking about this problem space. Now we have a robust ads system powering more than $1 billion in annualized run rate, with an LLM-based orchestrator running the ads flow. Codex was a fundamental force multiplier that allowed us to bootstrap our system to achieve this major usage milestone with unparalleled speed. From the start, we set up the team and development workflows to use Codex to rapidly build and scale the system. We built guardrails for Codex to reliably and safely ship code. In parallel, we set up data infrastructure plugins for Codex to massively tighten the loop of insight gathering and landing improvements to the system, including upcoming product features, quality improvements, and better system performance.

Industry observers note that the combination of our system’s boundaries (grounded in our advertising principles⁠) and our LLM-based orchestrator lets us make advertising useful without treating every conversation as an ad request. Looking ahead, we’ll continue to experiment with more dynamic ad formats to increase user value (e.g. giving users the ability to talk directly to businesses through ads) and advertiser value. The stack’s self-improving architecture, built on OpenAI models with continuous feedback loops, will accelerate our ability to keep improving relevance and personalization over time.

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (211 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Designer-RSI: Evolving Procedural Memory from User Traffic for Graphic Design Agent

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (211 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2609.22086v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deployed software agents face a continuous stream of user requests while their foundation-model weights remain frozen between releases. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) via external memory offers a practical path to continual adaptation, yet prior methods largely assume programmatic verifiers, cheap retries, or a single global prompt. Creative software breaks these assumptions, as open-ended visual briefs lack ground truth, VLM judges are noisy, and multi-step tool executions are costly and confounded by external assets. We present Designer-RSI, which evolves a modular skill bank from unlabeled design trajectories for an agent spanning over 230 raster, vector, and layout tools. Designer-RSI couples widening (acquiring new skills for recurring capability gaps) with deepening (revising failing skills by contrasting successful and failed runs), and screens updates through a Pareto-style matched replay gate that requires strict gains on sampled briefs without local regressions. Across held-out product briefs, eight external benchmarks, and two backbones, traffic-driven evolution outperforms static documentation skills, lifts execution success up to 99.8%, improves requirement fulfillment, and reaches up to a 67.6% blind win rate over the base agent. Ablations further show that skill acquisition and revision are strongly synergistic: neither suffices alone, and reliable gains require evolving coverage and execution quality together.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2609.11341v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multimodal brain state decoding has largely focused on fusing paired modalities for prediction, but has rarely explored how their correspondence can be further exploited to enrich training data and improve multimodal representation learning. To address this gap, we propose CoMA-DiT, a bidirectional cross-modal Diffusion Transformer for latent augmentation that treats paired modalities as sources of mutual generative supervision rather than merely as inputs to be fused. CoMA-DiT conditions velocity prediction on the paired modality through cross-modal attention and uses the shared hidden representation to construct reliability-gated residual augmentations. Experiments on multimodal auditory attention decoding and emotion recognition demonstrated that CoMA-DiT consistently outperformed more than 20 representative baselines, achieving absolute gains of 4.28 and 6.70 percentage points in accuracy and macro-F1 over the no-augmentation baseline, respectively. Extensive ablation, sensitivity, visualization, and interpretability analyses further demonstrated its robustness, generalizability, and ability to capture functionally relevant cross-modal interactions. These findings support a broader view of multimodal learning: Paired modalities can serve not only as inputs for fusion but also as supervision sources that augment one another.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cloudflare uses OpenAI Daybreak with live traffic and security signals to investigate vulnerabilities and propose fixes for customer review.

cyber threats blocked daily on average across Cloudflare’s network, Q1 2026.

reduced development resources to create a upcoming product.

It has been revealed that cloudflare operates one of the world’s largest networks and proxies roughly 20% of the web’s traffic. Organizations depend on that network to keep their applications and services secure, fast, and reliable.

Cloudflare combines OpenAI models accessed through Daybreak with its global network and threat context in Vulnerability Discovery and Remediation⁠(opens in a fresh window), an early-access service offered through Cloudflare Managed Defense. The models investigate code and assess potential vulnerabilities. Cloudflare adds live traffic data, security signals, and validation to prioritize findings and prepare proposed mitigations and patches for customers to review.

Codex extends OpenAI’s role across Cloudflare’s engineering organization, where developers use it to increase output and improve code quality.

It has been revealed that security teams face a constant stream of vulnerability information and alerts. Manually sifting through that data takes time and effort, leaving teams with less capacity to investigate and address critical problems. “Traditional security teams have a ton of useful data. They just don’t have the people and time to deal with it,” Anderson notes.

Cloudflare’s approach is to connect a vulnerability in source code to what is happening in production. Is the affected route active? Is it receiving suspicious traffic? Are existing security controls already protecting it? Those signals give security teams more context for deciding what to investigate first.

Through Vulnerability Discovery and Remediation⁠(opens in a upcoming window), Cloudflare uses OpenAI models accessed through Daybreak to investigate customer-authorized code, identify potential vulnerabilities, and check the evidence supporting each finding. The service prepares proposed code patches and, where appropriate, custom web application firewall rules to reduce exposure while developers review a fix. Cloudflare runs automated checks on these proposals, and its team reviews them before sharing them with customers.

For Cloudflare customers, the benefit is a clear path from identifying a vulnerability to protecting the affected application. The service gives them evidence to prioritize vulnerabilities, proposed edge protections to reduce exposure, and code fixes to review, while they retain control over which changes to implement.

Sources indicate that protecting applications also depends on the code teams write and maintain. Anderson connects Cloudflare’s use of Codex to greater developer productivity, better code quality, and fewer bugs introduced during development.

Anderson describes a recent rebuild the team had postponed. “We were putting off building it because we didn’t have the manpower to do it,” he indicates. With Codex scaling developer productivity, the question shifts from “Can we take this on?” to “Why not?”.

According to recent reports, anderson estimates that the work would have required months of sequencing and “maybe 10x more developers.” With Codex, a Cloudflare team of four developers took on the build. “We built it in three days, rolled it out and tested it, and spent $1,100 on tokens,” he says.

For Anderson, making AI part of everyday engineering means “rebuilding the internal process to build technology with machines in mind, not as a separate element, but as something that’s integrated into the build process.”.

Cloudflare’s early-access security service puts that approach into practice by connecting code investigation with production evidence and proposed actions customers can review. The goal is to give security teams the information they need to decide which vulnerabilities to prioritize and how to protect and fix affected applications, while customers retain control over changes.

Tech Report: Using thousands of AI agents to uncover new leads in biological data

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1099 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • How OpenAI, PerturbAI, and Scripps Research used distributed AI agents to help scientists identify promising research leads in data from millions of brain cells.
  • See how OpenAI, PerturbAI, and Scripps Research deployed thousands of AI agents in parallel to identify promising biological connections in complex data from millions of brain cells.
  • It has been revealed that what if scientists could uncover fresh clues about Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s in minutes instead of months?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How OpenAI, PerturbAI, and Scripps Research used distributed AI agents to help scientists identify promising research leads in data from millions of brain cells.

See how OpenAI, PerturbAI, and Scripps Research deployed thousands of AI agents in parallel to identify promising biological connections in complex data from millions of brain cells.

It has been revealed that what if scientists could uncover fresh clues about Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s in minutes instead of months? Working together, OpenAI, PerturbAI⁠(opens in a new window), and Scripps Research⁠(opens in a new window) used thousands of AI agents powered by GPT‑Rosalind⁠(opens in a new window) to analyze and interpret existing experimental data from millions of mouse brain cells⁠(opens in a new window) in just 32 minutes. The agents connected the effects of gene disruptions with findings from scientific literature, uncovering unexpected biological connections that can help scientists understand disease and identify research directions for new treatments. The work shows how AI can help researchers explore more of what large biological experiments reveal.

In a recent development, modern experiments generate far more data than scientists can thoroughly investigate. Researchers can now alter thousands of genes and measure their effects across millions of cells. But understanding what these results mean for human disease requires connecting complex experimental findings with decades of scattered scientific knowledge. This is where AI can help scientists uncover promising leads that might otherwise be missed.

The team divided the analysis among thousands of AI agents powered by GPT‑Rosalind, an approach we call distributed biological reasoning. The agents examined a whole-brain CRISPR atlas⁠(opens in a latest window), a dataset showing how gene disruptions affect different types of cells across the mouse brain. Each agent investigated a gene disruption, analyzed cellular responses, searched scientific literature, and proposed explanations for the results. Their reports were combined into a reasoning atlas linking genes, cellular effects, relevant publications, and possible biological mechanisms.

The research team estimated that comparable human analysis and literature review, conducted one perturbation at a time, would take months to a year. The agents reproduced findings from human analyses while uncovering additional leads. Their assessments of novelty and scientific value also aligned with judgments from blinded human experts. These findings help prioritize further experiments needed to test the proposed biological mechanisms.

Sources indicate that some of these insights point to latest leads for understanding brain disease. The agents identified unexpected differences in how two disease-linked genes affect brain cells differently, as well as a potential connection between cholesterol regulation and neurodegeneration. These findings could help scientists investigate how disease develops and where future treatments might intervene.

According to recent reports, researchers can begin exploring these findings today. The reasoning atlas is available⁠(opens in a fresh window), allowing scientists to compare related genes, investigate unexpected responses, and identify promising leads to pursue. New discoveries often emerge when researchers from different fields bring their expertise together and connect familiar ideas in unexpected ways. AI can significantly scale these connections by linking new data with knowledge scattered across disciplines. The opportunity goes beyond analyzing data faster. By combining AI with experimental biology, human expertise, and scientific literature, we can help scientists turn more of their data into testable ideas.

Some of an experiment’s most interesting clues lie outside the story scientists set out to investigate. In a dataset spanning thousands of perturbations, those clues can be easy to miss.

In a recent development, the agents identified an unexpected difference between Tsc1 and Tsc2, two genes that work together to control mTOR, a major regulator of cell growth, metabolism, and aging. Disrupting either gene had similar effects in several groups of neurons. But in the cerebellum, which helps coordinate movement, Tsc2 disruption altered the activity of dozens of genes involved in neuronal communication, while Tsc1 disruption produced little change.

That difference may be relevant to human disease. In people with tuberous sclerosis, abnormalities in the cerebellum are strongly linked to TSC2 mutations. While medicines that reduce mTOR activity can treat certain brain tumors and seizures, learning and behavioral difficulties associated with the disease remain challenging to address. The agents pinpointed a specific group of neurons and cellular changes worth investigating: which changes might existing medicines correct, and which might point to new treatment approaches? This gives researchers a more specific set of questions to test in the lab.

Could a single agent given the entire dataset do just as well as thousands of agents working in parallel? We tested this while keeping the model and resources fixed. As the workload grew, the single agent searched less of the literature, citing only 11 references at the largest workload, while the distributed agents cited more than 700 references. Human experts also preferred the distributed-agent interpretations.

In a recent development, scientists have limited time and often focus on the strongest signals in their data. Distributed agents can help examine a wider range of responses, including subtle or unexpected ones, and connect them with relevant scientific literature. Running the agents in parallel allows many perturbations to be investigated at once. This helps scientists explore more of what an experiment contains and identify promising leads that might otherwise be missed.

At the largest workload, distributed agents cited more than 700 references, compared with 11 for a single agent.

A finding becomes more valuable when it points to an experiment worth doing. The agents found one such lead in DCTN1, a gene whose mutations cause Perry syndrome, a neurodegenerative disease with Parkinson-like symptoms.

DCTN1 is involved in moving cargo inside neurons. In the whole-brain CRISPR atlas, disrupting Dctn1 increased the expression of genes involved in making cholesterol. The agents connected this observation with research suggesting that problems with cholesterol transport may cause cells to make more cholesterol. This raised a question for follow-up experiments: could DCTN1 disruption change how cholesterol is distributed within neurons, and could those changes contribute to neurodegeneration? If so, could restoring normal cholesterol distribution help protect neurons?

Recent findings suggest that human experts also considered this hypothesis novel, consequential and worth following up on. This example demonstrates how connecting an unexpected result with existing knowledge can turn a clue into a testable idea, and potentially a fresh direction for treating disease.

In blinded comparisons, human experts preferred distributed-agent reports over single-agent reports 75% of the time.

Scientists remain at the center of discovery. By uncovering more promising leads, AI can help researchers decide which ideas to pursue, design experiments, and interpret results. The goal is to turn more of the information in biological experiments into knowledge that, over time, can help guide the development of better medicines.

#39192. Support Topology and Gradient Mixing in Sinkhorn Layers

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (234 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Support Topology and Gradient Mixing in Sinkhorn Layers

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (234 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2609.07954v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sinkhorn attention layers normalize weights over a fixed sparse mask by alternating row and column scaling. When training these layers, sparse masks are usually judged by their edge count, graph diameter, or forward reachability. We show that the sparsity pattern and marginal budgets also govern how gradients flow backward through the scaling steps. Differentiating one row-column cycle on column log-potentials yields an explicit row-stochastic Markov kernel built from the two half-step transport looks, which reduces to a reversible two-step random walk at a balanced fixed point. Because potentials are defined only up to additive constants on each connected component, reverse-mode gradients propagate as zero-sum vectors whose total-variation norm contracts at a rate given by the kernel's Dobrushin coefficient. This coefficient bounds both unrolled backpropagation and implicit-differentiation truncation error. Crucially, graph connectivity alone does not prevent gradient trapping: we prove a face-lattice dichotomy showing that a mask and marginals guarantee score-uniform one-step contraction if and only if every nonempty face of the transportation polytope retains pairwise two-hop column overlap; otherwise, large learned scores can push the contraction rate arbitrarily close to one. We extend this criterion to multi-layer schedules, prove exact one-sweep mixing for coordinate-factorized and butterfly masks, and derive closed-form bounds for expanders, local bands, and global hub tokens. Deterministic numerical checks verify our finite-difference adjoints, canonical sparse masks, adversarial score limits, and spectral formulas.

#39191. Do Latent World Models Really Select the Right Actions?

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (193 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Do Latent World Models Really Select the Right Actions?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (193 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2609.05461v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper highlights that the planning success of a latent world model does not reveal how well its score selects actions. Latent world models score candidate action sequences by the distance between their predicted embeddings and the embedding of a goal image, and their strong planning results are naturally read as evidence that this score picks good actions. Our study is simple: we take two released models, JEPA-WM and DINO-WM, execute the action sequences their planners consider, and compare what the score prefers with what actually happens. We make two observations. First, the score is informative but unreliable: it picks better actions than chance, yet it often passes over a successful sequence that the search has already found. Second, planning still succeeds, helped by a wider search and by replanning from fresh observations. With the released search budget, PointMaze planning succeeds in 91% of episodes, yet the top-scored candidate at the end of a search is no more likely to succeed than a random one. These observations suggest that the score should be measured directly, next to the success rate.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From local businesses to global brands, more advertisers can now reach people as they explore, compare and decide what to buy in ChatGPT.

More than 1.2 billion people use ChatGPT each week to explore ideas, compare options and make decisions. Ads can help people discover products and services that fit their needs, including options they might not have found otherwise.

Since we launched ads just over eight months ago, over 100,000 advertisers have run campaigns on ChatGPT. Today, we’re expanding ChatGPT Ads to 26 additional countries, extending availability to 89 countries worldwide. This launch builds on our recent expansions across Europe and Southeast Asia and Taiwan.

Advertising helps support free and low-cost access to ChatGPT for people around the world. Our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. Ads will appear only on the Free and Go plans. Plus, Pro, and Enterprise subscriptions will remain ad-free.

It has been revealed that following our introduces in Mexico and Brazil, we’re bringing ChatGPT Ads to 14 more Latin American countries, including Argentina, Chile, Colombia, and Peru. We’re also launching in more markets across Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia, including Nigeria, South Africa, Serbia, Ukraine, Cambodia, Bangladesh, and Pakistan.

Advertisers can access ChatGPT Ads in these countries through technology partners or self-service access through Ads Manager⁠(opens in a fresh window).

In ChatGPT, people can explain what they’re looking for, ask follow-up questions, and refine their options through conversation. Someone training for their first marathon might start by exploring meal ideas for race week, then narrow their options based on their dietary preferences and how much time they have to cook. An ad relevant to that conversation could introduce them to a grocery delivery service they hadn’t considered.

For local businesses, regional brands, and international companies, ChatGPT Ads gives businesses a way to introduce their products during these moments of consideration, when people are still evaluating their options and deciding what’s right for them.

Protecting the trust people place in ChatGPT is foundational to our approach to advertising.

Guided by OpenAI’s ads principles, we keep conversations private from advertisers and do not sell customer data. Ads in ChatGPT are clearly labeled and separate from ChatGPT’s answers, and advertising does not influence the answers ChatGPT provides.

Our goal is to make ads useful to people as they pursue their goals and make decisions—and effective for the businesses that advertise with us.

Our focus remains expanding access to AI while staying true to our principles.

It has been revealed that with ChatGPT Ads now available in 89 countries, our next phase of growth will include the development of additional formats, objectives, buying options, and measurement capabilities. We are also continuing to explore newly introduced ways for businesses to interact with consumers in more native ways in ChatGPT.

As more people turn to ChatGPT to explore needs, evaluate options, and make decisions, we see an opportunity to help them discover products and services—and to help businesses of every size grow and thrive.

Businesses interested in advertising on ChatGPT can learn more at ads.openai.com⁠(opens in a latest window).

A Table Is Worth 64 Tokens: Pixel-level Compression for Multi-Table Document Question Answering

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (189 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2608.26949v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Answering questions over real-world documents requires processing long inputs that interleave text with tables. Optical context compression, which represents context as images, promises to reduce token cost, but its effect on table understanding remains unclear. We study pixel-level table compression for question answering over documents with multiple tables, evaluating seven VLMs across two benchmarks and five visual-token budgets. At moderate budgets, table images match html in accuracy with fewer tokens, but aggressive downscaling makes models reason longer without recovering accuracy, eroding the savings. Yet even at 64 visual tokens per table, tables preserve enough signal to identify whether they are relevant to a question. We exploit this asymmetry with a training-free, two-stage method: the model first identifies the tables needed to answer a question from a pixel-compressed context, and then reasons over those tables at native resolution. On long financial documents, it uses 41% fewer tokens than single-step QA over native-resolution tables while gaining 5 accuracy points, and 21% fewer than the most efficient compressed configuration at no accuracy cost. It also still saves tokens when applied to retrieved context.

Depth Enables Local Entropy: Quadratic Depth Dependence in Deep Variation-Norm ReLU Regression

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (190 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2608.17434v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: How small can a layer-sum variation budget be while deep ReLU regression keeps a statistical complexity quadratic in depth? We study Gaussian regression on the circle over compositions of $L$ vector-valued ReLU blocks of width $w$, whose second-order variation costs sum to at most $A$. With unit output bound and noise level, a budget $CLw^\varepsilon$ already forces minimax risk $\Omega(\varepsilon^2\min\{1,L^2w^2\log w/n\})$ for each fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,2]$ and $L\gtrsim1/\varepsilon$. This is far below the budget of order $Lw^2$ needed when every layer carries the full gain. When $L\gtrsim\log w$, a budget $CL$ forces risk $\Omega(\min\{1,L^2w^2/(n\log w)\})$, and over a wide range of sample sizes no budget below a small multiple of $L$ reaches this risk. Conversely, every function in the class has derivative variation at most $2(A/L)^L$, independently of the width, and in a low-budget regime the minimax risk matches that of a one-dimensional second-variation ball of radius $(A/L)^L$. The budget thus moves the class from the behavior of a one-dimensional smoothness ball to statistical complexity quadratic in depth, and a budget linear in depth already suffices for the latter.

Latest Update: DiSCO: Defending text-to-image generation through distribution-guided contrastive prompt optimization

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (222 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2608.17067v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As text-to-image generative models advance, they raise critical safety concerns, particularly the generation of Not-Safe-For-Work (NSFW) content such as violence and nudity, further exacerbated by red-teaming adversarial attacks. Existing defenses predominantly operate under white-box assumptions, relying on text encoder optimization, weight editing, or inference-time intervention, and fundamentally cannot scale to proprietary models. Black-box alternatives based on LLM prompt rewriting offer broader applicability, yet fail in a critical regime we identify as the \textit{benign adversarial} problem: prompts that are linguistically safe but still trigger harmful generation due to the model's learned data distribution. We propose DiSCO, a zero-shot, strictly black-box defense that operates entirely at the prompt level as a plug-and-play module, requiring no model retraining, fine-tuning, or access to model internals. DiSCO performs distribution-guided suffix expansion via beam search, optimized through contrastive scoring over safe and unsafe image pools generated by the target model itself, with iterative adaptive feedback until safe content is produced. We demonstrate that DiSCO consistently enhances the safety of both undefended and defended models on the I2P benchmark under multiple red-teaming attacks, achieving 37.7% and 25.13% ASR reduction, respectively, while maintaining semantic fidelity and improving image coherence. As a black-box, architecture-agnostic module, DiSCO can be readily applied to any text-to-image system without necessitating any changes to the model itself.

Patch the Planet: global response coordination as agents uncover critical vulnerabilities

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1871 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the past two months, we led a coalition of maintainers, researchers, and security providers to address critical vulnerabilities in PHP, an open-source programming language used to run websites and web applications.
  • In a recent development, for organizations using PHP, the priority now is applying the fixes.
  • Sources indicate that given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the past two months, we led a coalition of maintainers, researchers, and security providers to address critical vulnerabilities in PHP, an open-source programming language used to run websites and web applications. Calif identified a critical flaw using GPT‑5.6 Sol as part of our Patch the Planet⁠(opens in a new window) initiative, with Wiz also independently discovering and reporting both vulnerabilities. PHP’s maintainers led the fixes and release, with our teams and partners like Wiz, Cloudflare, and others contributing research, technical support, and coordination to prepare protections ahead of disclosure.

In a recent development, for organizations using PHP, the priority now is applying the fixes. We’re sharing a PHP version checker as a Codex skill⁠(opens in a upcoming window) to help operators identify potentially vulnerable PHP versions and, alongside PHP’s and their providers’ guidance, determine which updates apply.

Sources indicate that given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory. It highlights how AI can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits.

To our knowledge, frontier AI found these vulnerabilities before attackers did, opening a Defender’s Window for maintainers and security providers to prepare fixes and protections ahead of disclosure.

To help more defenders use these capabilities, we’ve committed $1 billion in subsidized Daybreak access through Daybreak for Frontline Defenders, focused on organizations with limited security resources protecting essential services.

As significant as they are, these bugs are among several significant vulnerabilities we’ve already found and are working to fix, and we expect similar findings to increase sharply in the coming months. Drawing on our experience thus far, we’re sharing a proposed approach, appropriate for the AI era, to responding to critical vulnerabilities in widely used software, and we’re asking the security community to help improve this framework. It brings together our models, security expertise, and maintainers to help turn findings into protection and build a response that can scale as AI capabilities advance.

Getting a fix into use can mean adapting it for older releases, preparing provider mitigations, and updating systems across many organizations. A repeatable process helps those teams act quickly as more vulnerabilities are discovered.

Industry observers note that through Patch the Planet, we contributed security expertise and model access to support the PHP response, and worked with maintainers and research partners to test fixes and prepare guidance. We also helped coordinate with infrastructure providers on protections for affected systems and engaged government cyber agencies to help guidance reach critical organizations. This supported the maintainer-led response and helped other defenders prepare.

According to recent reports, for some findings, researchers can work directly with the software’s maintainers to investigate the issue and develop a fix. Others need a wider response because they affect many products or because distributors and service providers need time (which may be in short supply if frontier capabilities are not too far ahead of those that are broadly available) to prepare updates and protections. In those cases, the proposed framework can help maintainers identify who needs to be involved and coordinate the work. The response can involve five stages:.

Industry observers note that validate and fix the upstream vulnerability. The maintainer, researchers, and essential technical partners confirm the finding, assess its impact, and develop and test a fix. This process includes adversarial testing with frontier models to look for ways around the patch and related variants of the vulnerability.

It has been revealed that give affected organizations time to act. We propose a framework for considering which organizations need advance information to prepare protections, while maintainers decide whom to involve. We help with outreach, information-sharing agreements, and coordination between teams. A distributor might adapt a fix for an older release, a hosting provider might test a mitigation, and a security provider might prepare detection or prevention measures, including web application firewall (WAF) rules.

Recent findings suggest that coordinate with government partners to help protect critical systems. Government agencies play an essential role in coordinating a wider response and helping security guidance reach organizations responsible for critical infrastructure and other essential services. In the case of PHP, we worked, in collaboration with our partners, to engage with multiple parts of the U.S. government, including the White House’s Super Intelligence Force, the Office of the National Cyber Director (ONCD), the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), as well as international partners to support that effort.

Prepare updates across affected products. As the fix, guidance, and disclosure plans become stable, maintainers can involve additional distributors, hosting and service providers, response teams, and operators to prepare updates and address gaps in coverage.

Recent findings suggest that once a patch is available, publish guidance and support deployment. Public guidance helps people assess their exposure, find authoritative updates or interim mitigations, and check that a fix is running. The response continues as operators deploy updates and report where they need help.

The proposed framework considers an organization’s protective role, including protecting its own systems and customers, the time needed to act, and its ability to handle sensitive information. The same criteria would apply to comparable organizations, with maintainers deciding whom to involve ahead of disclosure.

Each participant receives the information needed to carry out their protective work, from network logs with indicators of compromise to more sensitive working proof-of-concept exploits. Even limited details can reveal a vulnerability, so we weigh the risk of sharing them against the protection they enable.

Teams following this framework would work with maintainers to give defenders time to prepare and reassess the timeline if there’s active exploitation in the wild, a leak, a revealing public patch, or increased risk to consumers from stalled remediation.

The Patch the Planet website⁠(opens in a new window) brings together public disclosures and guidance to help operators identify affected systems, find the right update, and verify that the updated software is running properly. For PHP, it points to the maintainers’ official patch and upgrade instructions and our partners’ technical research. The guidance also covers interim mitigations, when to involve a provider or expert, and backup and recovery. Interim protections can reduce risk, but we’ll make their limits and operational tradeoffs clear.

Operators can use CISA’s guidance on prioritization and remediation⁠(opens in a new window) to assess how quickly to act based on exposure, exploitation, and potential impact. That may mean emergency patching, immediate mitigation, or a planned enhancement, alongside forensic triage where warranted to assess whether systems have already been compromised. Priorities should be reassessed as conditions change, with a clear path to lasting remediation.

Global coordination depends on the people who maintain the software. Many projects are run by small teams that review security reports alongside routine development. Those teams need help separating new issues from duplicates, assessing impact, and testing fixes across supported releases. We support that work with funding, access to capable models, and hands-on engineering help.

It has been revealed that powerful AI capabilities are advancing across the industry, and we expect AI to play a growing role in helping defenders find vulnerabilities, monitor systems, and respond to threats. We’re investing in models, tools, and partnerships to help defenders put those capabilities to work.

Our investments include subscriptions for all maintainers through Codex for OSS and direct sponsorship of projects such as the Rust Foundation⁠(opens in a upcoming window) for maintainers and technical work. Each project sets its own priorities. Reusable tests and security workflows can reduce the effort needed to handle future findings. Open-source projects can apply to Patch the Planet⁠(opens in a new window) for hands-on support.

Recent findings suggest that we’re also calibrating additional blocking classifiers for Daybreak to help reduce the potential for misuse. This involves difficult tradeoffs: safeguards intended to prevent abuse can also block legitimate security work. Broad access to capable models and effective protections against misuse are both critical. Our aim is to preserve the capabilities defenders need to find and fix vulnerabilities while limiting harmful use. We’ll continue refining that balance as capabilities advance and we learn from how these tools are used.

Recent findings suggest that as models become more capable, the opportunity extends beyond finding and fixing individual vulnerabilities. We want to help engineers build more secure software from the start. Improvements to a widely used component can prevent bugs or limit their impact across many products and services.

Recent findings suggest that AI can help engineers understand existing code, prepare changes, and develop tests, while maintainers and security experts verify that those changes preserve the behavior consumers depend on. We see opportunities in several areas:.

Secure code from the start. Coding models can help developers choose safer defaults, use security libraries correctly, and catch risky patterns as they write. Preventing vulnerabilities during development means fewer emergency fixes for maintainers and people.

Memory-safe software. Moving critical components to memory-safe languages can eliminate common classes of memory errors. AI can help with migrations, with tests and expert review to check behavior and compatibility.

Formal verification. Mathematical proofs can show that critical components satisfy specified security properties under stated assumptions. Applying these methods to widely used components could help rule out classes of vulnerabilities across the services and critical infrastructure that depend on them.

Stronger isolation. Systems need protection against vulnerabilities that have not yet been found or fixed. Running software that processes untrusted files, images, or media in tightly restricted sandboxes can limit the damage if it is compromised. AI can help engineers test and strengthen widely used sandboxing technologies, improving protections across many applications.

We’re sharing our approach so maintainers, researchers, response teams, providers, and operators can help make it workable. We want to understand where it would help, where it could add delay or burden, and what we’ve missed. Examples from past disclosures would be especially useful.

We’re particularly interested in:.

Sources indicate that disclosure windows. How much time do maintainers, operators, and defenders need to prepare and deploy reliable fixes? What evidence should trigger earlier disclosure, especially when some customers can be protected sooner than others?

Emergency patching. When, if ever, should governments or other operators use a vulnerability to patch systems they own or are authorized to manage after losing administrative access? What safeguards should apply? We can imagine an end-state of internet-wide always-on scanning for known vulnerabilities, and either notifying site owners when one is detected or patching the system.

According to recent reports, early notice. Who needs advance warning to take a useful protective action, including defenders we might miss? When do staged notifications work better than notifying a wider group at once, and how should we weigh coverage against leak risk?

According to recent reports, secure-by-default software packages. How can we help identify and fix vulnerabilities in downstream packages while upstream fixes are pending, or backport fixes to older versions that no longer receive security updates? What testing and maintenance would make these packages reliable options when a timely upgrade isn’t feasible?

We also welcome recommendations for independent security experts who can review the approach, challenge its assumptions, and identify gaps. Your input will help us refine the response and prioritize support. Share your feedback here⁠(opens in a new window).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • OpenAI and Google Cloud⁠(opens in a fresh window) are partnering to bring OpenAI’s frontier models and Codex⁠(opens in a new window) agentic workflows into Google Cloud’s Model Garden.
  • Google Cloud’s longstanding investment in machine learning and AI has made it a destination for AI workloads and the developers and data scientists building them.
  • For organizations in regulated industries, deploying AI requires control over who can access sensitive data and how it is used.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI and Google Cloud⁠(opens in a fresh window) are partnering to bring OpenAI’s frontier models and Codex⁠(opens in a new window) agentic workflows into Google Cloud’s Model Garden. The integration will give customers native access to these models to power complex agentic workflows at scale, backed by Google Cloud’s data governance and high-performance infrastructure.

Google Cloud’s longstanding investment in machine learning and AI has made it a destination for AI workloads and the developers and data scientists building them. Bringing OpenAI models to its model garden gives these teams access to OpenAI’s frontier models within the environment where they already work, enabling enterprises to modernize their software development lifecycle, build agentic workflows, and change how people work.

For organizations in regulated industries, deploying AI requires control over who can access sensitive data and how it is used. The integration will pair OpenAI’s frontier models with Google Cloud’s built-in access controls, centralized data governance, and high-performance infrastructure to support demanding enterprise workloads.

Sources indicate that google Cloud customers will be able to purchase OpenAI frontier models via model garden, transacted through the Google Cloud Marketplace. Enterprises with Google Cloud spend commitments will be able to draw down their GCP commitments for these purchases.

It has been revealed that additionally, OpenAI models will soon be available in Google Antigravity and the Gemini Agent, providing enterprise customers with model choice flexibility and the best model for each task. By expanding access through Google Cloud, we are giving enterprises greater choice in how they discover and use frontier models, with a path from evaluation to broader adoption.

General availability is planned in the coming weeks. Request access to OpenAI on Google Cloud here.

Microsoft remains OpenAI’s primary cloud partner.
